title: Application API reference
description: Reference Gonex construction, module registration, typed routing, lifecycle and resource APIs.
text:
These decisions began as the phase 0 contract and now describe the implemented application API. Historical results remain in the phase reports(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/README.mdimplementation-record).


 Module and toolchain

The Go module is github.com/amkargar/gonex; the product name is goNex. The repository baseline is Go 1.27.2. Exact dependency versions are pinned in go.mod(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/go.mod). See release policy(/docs/main/release/) for configured and verified platforms.

 Construction and registration

- gonex.New(config.Config) (app.App, error) validates settings without binding ports.
- Module.Register(Registrar) error declares a module's routes and resources.
- App.Register(...Module) error registers explicitly in argument order, atomically per call.
- Registration freezes at startup. A failed registration call leaves the application unchanged.
- Registrar.Handle(method, path string, handlers ...gin.HandlerFunc) error is a raw Gin escape hatch. Use typed HTTP registration for public contracts.

 Routing and contracts

Route identity is the uppercase method plus full path. Duplicate and incompatible wildcard routes fail before serving. Runtime health/readiness and enabled document paths reject conflicting registrations.

http.Routes groups concise typed declarations such as http.Get(path, handler).Name(operationID). Handler request and response types are inferred. The lower-level http.Register API remains available and builds the same typed endpoint contract. Request origins, supported validation constraints and schema projection are checked together. Contracts detach mutable metadata at registration. Raw Gin routes are not included in OpenAPI.

HTTP versions are explicit adapter packages. gRPC remains optional, with versioned Protobuf packages and independently managed servers/clients. See HTTP contracts(/docs/main/http/) and gRPC(/docs/main/grpc/).

 Resource ownership

Registrar.Manage(Resource) error owns resources implementing Start(context.Context) error and Close(context.Context) error. Registration order determines startup order; close runs in reverse. Dependencies register before their consumers. An optional Errors channel reports asynchronous failure to App.Run.

Registrar.Check(name, func(context.Context) error) adds a named dependency readiness check. Resources may also implement Ready(context.Context) error. Application callbacks must honor context cancellation.

 Lifecycle guarantees

| API | Behavior |
|---|---|
| App.Start(ctx) | Starts managed resources and binds the HTTP listener synchronously |
| App.Run(ctx) | Starts, waits for cancellation/failure and shuts down within the configured budget |
| App.Shutdown(ctx) | Drains HTTP and closes resources; repeated calls are safe |
| App.Ready(ctx) | Checks running state and registered dependency readiness |

States are created, registered, starting, running, stopping and stopped. A stopped instance cannot restart. Configuration includes address, middleware, exposure switches and read/write/idle/shutdown timeouts. Zero durations use defaults; negative values fail. See modules(/docs/main/modules/) and operations(/docs/main/operations/).

title: Application architecture
description: Structure a Gonex application around plain Go business services, explicit modules and optional HTTP, database and gRPC adapters.
text:
Start small

Your first application can fit in one main.go. As it grows, organize your own business modules; you do not need to edit the Gonex package. The project structure guide(/docs/main/project-structure/) shows concrete file responsibilities.

 Compose modules explicitly

A module implements Register(app.Registrar) error. The executable constructs the application and registers its modules:

go
a, err := gonex.New(config.Config)
if err != nil  return err 
if err = a.Register(users.Module, catalog.Module); err != nil  return err 
return a.Run(ctx)


This excerpt assumes your application defines the two module types and has an existing context. See the complete quick-start program(/docs/main/quick-start/) for a runnable single-module example.

 Keep business rules in your service

Your HTTP handler translates requests into service calls. Your service accepts ordinary Go values and depends on small local interfaces. GORM and gRPC implementations sit behind those interfaces when needed.

| Layer in your application | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| Service | Business rules and consumer-owned dependency interfaces |
| HTTP adapter | Request/response schemas.go, validation and status mapping |
| Database adapter | GORM models, queries and persistence mapping |
| gRPC adapter | Versioned Protobuf mapping and remote calls |
| Executable/module registration | Construction, configuration and resource composition |

Use a modular monolith first when that fits your application. Independent services and gRPC are optional; there is no requirement to adopt them for an HTTP API.

 Let the application own resources

Managed resources expose Start(context.Context) error and Close(context.Context) error. Register dependencies before consumers and honor cancellation. Gonex starts them in registration order and closes them in reverse during shutdown. See modules and lifecycle(/docs/main/modules/) and operations(/docs/main/operations/).

 Framework internals are a separate path

If your goal is to change how Gonex itself registers routes, generates contracts or scaffolds code, use Framework internals(/docs/main/contribute/architecture/). This main documentation describes how to build your own application with the public API.

 Local microservices workflow

Follow First microservice call(/docs/main/microservices-quickstart/) for explicit client profiles and wiring, dev/doctor and independently published contracts. Existing generated paths and TLS defaults are retained. Compatibility(/docs/main/microservices-compatibility/) explains skeleton/example/raw profiles, version coexistence and generation checks.

title: Build a REST API
description: Build create, list and get user endpoints in a CLI-generated Gonex app, using schemas.go validation, explicit services and OpenAPI.
text:
Create a separate API project

Use Go 1.27.2. Start in an empty parent directory, not inside the quick-start shop:

sh
go install github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@3ca54b46cb42
gonex new api --module example.com/shop
cd api
go mod tidy
go tool gonex create module users --transport none


We start with a generated business module and add its handwritten HTTP adapter below. --transport none avoids a starter /users route while we define the complete resource contract. The normal HTTP scaffold is covered in Quick start(/docs/main/quick-start/).

Keep the generated main.go, config/config.go, modules/registry_gen.go and .gonex.json. Replace the generated users service/module files with the following code, create modules/users/http/, and replace the starter service test with your own tests. The complete tested source(https://github.com/amkargar/GoNex-website/tree/main/examples/api) includes these exact files and API tests. You can copy the files into your generated app; cloning either repository is unnecessary.

 Define the business service

Replace modules/users/service.go. This example stores users in memory with concurrent access protection. Data is lost on restart; add a repository for persistence.

go
package users

import (
	"context"
	"strconv"
	"sync"

	apperrors "github.com/amkargar/gonex/errors"
	"github.com/amkargar/gonex/observability"
)

type User struct ID, Name, Email string 
type Service struct 
	mu    sync.RWMutex
	users User


func NewService() Service  return &Service 

func (s Service) Create(ctx context.Context, name, email string) (User, error) 
	if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil 
		return User, err
	
	s.mu.Lock()
	for _, u := range s.users 
		if u.Email == email 
			s.mu.Unlock()
			return User, apperrors.New(apperrors.Conflict, "email already exists")
		
	
	user := UserID: strconv.Itoa(len(s.users) + 1), Name: name, Email: email
	s.users = append(s.users, user)
	s.mu.Unlock()
	observability.Logger(ctx, nil).InfoContext(ctx, "user created", "module", "users", "user_id", user.ID)
	return user, nil

func (s Service) List(ctx context.Context) (User, error) 
	if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil 
		return nil, err
	
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	return append(User(nil), s.users...), nil

func (s Service) Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (User, error) 
	if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil 
		return User, err
	
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()
	for _, u := range s.users 
		if u.ID == id 
			return u, nil
		
	
	return User, apperrors.New(apperrors.NotFound, "user not found")



 Define request and response schemas

Create modules/users/http/schemas.go. The body wrapper declares JSON binding; validation rejects invalid names/emails before the service is called.

go
package usershttp

type CreateBody struct 
	Name  string json:"name" validate:"required,min=2,max=80"
	Email string json:"email" validate:"required,email,max=254"

type CreateRequest struct 
	Body CreateBody body:"true"

type GetRequest struct 
	ID string path:"id" validate:"required"

type UserResponse struct 
	ID    string json:"id"
	Name  string json:"name"
	Email string json:"email"

type ListResponse struct 
	Items UserResponse json:"items"


type ListRequest struct


 Map requests to actions

Create modules/users/http/handlers.go. The HTTP adapter accepts explicit actions and does not import database models.

go
package usershttp

import "context"

type Actions struct 
	Create func(context.Context, string, string) (UserResponse, error)
	List   func(context.Context) (UserResponse, error)
	Get    func(context.Context, string) (UserResponse, error)

type Handler struct Actions Actions 

func (h Handler) Create(ctx context.Context, in CreateRequest) (UserResponse, error) 
	return h.Actions.Create(ctx, in.Body.Name, in.Body.Email)

func (h Handler) List(ctx context.Context, _ ListRequest) (ListResponse, error) 
	items, err := h.Actions.List(ctx)
	return ListResponseItems: items, err

func (h Handler) Get(ctx context.Context, in GetRequest) (UserResponse, error) 
	return h.Actions.Get(ctx, in.ID)



 Register typed endpoints

Create modules/users/http/routes.go. Use concise typed declarations. Handler input/output types are inferred; Post defaults to 201 and Get to 200. Declare each operation name and domain error so OpenAPI matches runtime behavior.

go
package usershttp

import transport "github.com/amkargar/gonex/http"

func Register(r transport.EndpointRegistrar, actions Actions) error 
	h := HandlerActions: actions
	return transport.Routes(r,
		transport.Post("/api/users", h.Create).
			Name("createUser").
			Summary(createSummary).
			Tags("users").
			Errors(409),
		transport.Get("/api/users", h.List).
			Name("listUsers").
			Summary(listSummary).
			Tags("users"),
		transport.Get("/api/users/:id", h.Get).
			Name("getUser").
			Summary(getSummary).
			Tags("users").
			Errors(404),
	)



Create modules/users/http/openapi.go:

go
package usershttp

const (
	createSummary = "Create a user"
	listSummary   = "List users"
	getSummary    = "Get a user"
)


 Wire the module

Replace modules/users/module.go. Explicit mapping keeps service values separate from HTTP DTOs. The existing generated module registry already registers users.Module; do not edit it.

go
package users

import (
	"context"
	usershttp "example.com/shop/modules/users/http"
	"github.com/amkargar/gonex/app"
)

type Module struct Service Service 

func (m Module) Register(r app.Registrar) error 
	service := m.Service
	if service == nil 
		service = NewService()
	
	response := func(u User) usershttp.UserResponse 
		return usershttp.UserResponseID: u.ID, Name: u.Name, Email: u.Email
	
	return usershttp.Register(r, usershttp.Actions
		Create: func(ctx context.Context, name, email string) (usershttp.UserResponse, error) 
			u, err := service.Create(ctx, name, email)
			return response(u), err
		,
		Get: func(ctx context.Context, id string) (usershttp.UserResponse, error) 
			u, err := service.Get(ctx, id)
			return response(u), err
		,
		List: func(ctx context.Context) (usershttp.UserResponse, error) 
			users, err := service.List(ctx)
			items := make(usershttp.UserResponse, 0, len(users))
			for _, u := range users 
				items = append(items, response(u))
			
			return items, err
		,
	)



 Replace the starter test

Replace modules/users/service_test.go (the original test calls the starter Message method):

go
package users

import (
	"context"
	"sync"
	"testing"
)

func TestConcurrentCreateAndRead(t testing.T) 
	s := NewService()
	ctx := context.Background()
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for i := 0; i < 10; i++ 
		wg.Add(1)
		go func()  defer wg.Done(); _, _ = s.Create(ctx, "Ada", "ada@example.com"); _, _ = s.List(ctx) ()
	
	wg.Wait()
	users, err := s.List(ctx)
	if err != nil || len(users) != 1 
		t.Fatal(users, err)
	
	if _, err = s.Get(ctx, users0.ID); err != nil 
		t.Fatal(err)
	



 Run your API

sh
go mod tidy
go tool gonex check
go tool gonex run


The terminal shows your local server and OpenAPI URLs. The standard generated configuration reads HTTP_ADDRESS and log settings; see logging(/docs/main/logging/).

Create a user (POSIX shell; on PowerShell use curl.exe with the appropriate JSON quoting or Invoke-RestMethod):

sh
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com"'


The response is 201 Created:

json
"id":"1","name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com"


sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/users
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/users/1
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/openapi.json


| Request | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| GET /api/users | 200, an items array, including an empty array before creation |
| POST valid user | 201, created user |
| POST same email twice | 409 conflict |
| POST invalid name/email | 422 validation error |
| POST malformed JSON or unknown fields | 400 invalid request |
| GET unknown user | 404 not found |

The service emits a user created event with module/user ID; its request ID matches the HTTP completion event. Default request logs omit body, token and query-string values. Business log fields are explicit.

 Next steps

This is an explicit resource API, not an automatic ModelViewSet. It has no authentication, pagination, update/delete actions or persistent storage. Add those deliberately using security(/docs/main/security/), database adapters(/docs/main/database/) and HTTP contracts(/docs/main/http/). Connect a frontend through the JSON API(/docs/main/frontend/).

title: CLI reference
description: Reference Gonex commands for safe project scaffolding, modules, API versions, gRPC generation and database migrations.
text:
Install and create a project

Follow installation(/docs/main/installation/) for the pinned CLI. Run gonex new shop --module example.com/acme/shop, then cd shop and go mod tidy. Continue with go tool gonex inside the generated application. The command forms below use the executable name; prefix it with go tool in your project.

 Project creation

sh
gonex new NAME --module IMPORT_PATH --framework-version VERSION --arch monolith|microservices --dry-run


The architecture defaults to monolith. The framework version defaults to the installed CLI’s resolved module version, including Go pseudo-versions. A CLI built locally must receive an explicit valid --framework-version. The destination must not exist.

Install with go install github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@3ca54b46cb42 for this snapshot, or pin a reviewed commit/published tag. Generated apps include a tool directive: inside the app use go tool gonex for the commands below. Microservices workspaces also have a root tool module; run go mod tidy there after creation.

 Modules and services

sh
gonex create module NAME --transport http|none|grpc|http,grpc --http-version vN --db --service NAME --dry-run
gonex create service NAME --dry-run
gonex create client PROVIDER --service CONSUMER --module MODULE --version v1 --dry-run


| Option | Behavior |
|---|---|
| --transport | Defaults to http; none creates only the business core |
| --http-version | Starts an HTTP module directly in a version package, without legacy routes |
| --db | Adds a store interface, GORM adapter, model and explicit migration |
| --service | Selects the owning service in a microservices workspace |
| --version | Selects the provider's Protobuf API major for a client skeleton |
| --dry-run | Validates and prints the proposed plan without changing project files |

create service requires a microservices workspace. A client skeleton uses real generated service constructors but leaves domain mapping and injection to the developer. Run go mod tidy in each affected module after adding dependencies.

 Adapter changes

sh
gonex module version NAME --http vN --policy preserve|replace --prefix PATH --service NAME --dry-run
gonex module enable NAME --grpc --service NAME --dry-run


Versioning defaults to preserve and /api/vN. replace stops registering legacy routes while retaining their source. Existing version packages are not overwritten. Enabling gRPC preserves handwritten source and requires the supported injectable service factory. See HTTP versions(/docs/main/versioning/) and microservices(/docs/main/microservices/).

 Run and verify

sh
gonex run --service NAME
gonex build --os OS --arch ARCH --out FILE --service NAME
gonex check --service NAME
gonex --help
gonex --version


run invokes the Go executable path for the project; the application displays its bound address and writes structured lifecycle/request logs. See logging(/docs/main/logging/). build writes an application executable; check runs tests, vet and package compilation. Child command failures preserve their exit codes. A workspace command must identify a service when selection is ambiguous.

 OpenAPI

sh
gonex openapi generate --out openapi.json --http-version vN --service NAME --dry-run
gonex openapi validate --file openapi.json --against BASELINE --service NAME


Generation executes the project's initialization/export path without starting listeners, validates the result and writes the output. It exports the legacy document unless --http-version selects a registered major. Validation is offline; --against additionally runs conservative compatibility checks against a baseline. A generation dry run does not execute project code.

 Database migrations

sh
gonex db migrate --service NAME --dry-run
gonex db status --service NAME --dry-run


Configure DATABASE_URL and, where needed, DATABASE_DIALECT in the executable's environment. Migrations are explicit; serving does not automatically change schemas. Dry runs do not connect to the database. See database behavior(/docs/main/database/).

 Protobuf contracts

sh
gonex grpc generate --dry-run
gonex grpc check


Run from a supported project/workspace, service or contracts root. Generation compiles and checks contracts, then invokes pinned official plugins and stages the resulting files. Dry runs omit plugins and writes. check compares descriptors to the stored baseline. Neither command substitutes for the release workflow's Buf gate; see gRPC contracts(/docs/main/grpc/).

 Generator safety

Generators plan and validate paths and collisions before writes. They reject traversal, symlinks and handwritten-file overwrites, hash-check tool-owned registries and support dry runs. .gonex.json records ownership metadata; do not delete it to bypass a conflict.

New projects use a staged rename. Existing projects use an exclusive lock, staging and rollback on ordinary application errors; multi-file updates are not power-loss atomic. After an interrupted process, inspect .gonex.lock and proposed changes before recovering. See getting started(/docs/main/quick-start/generator-safety).

 Upgrade your application dependency

Select a reviewed target with go get -tool github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@TARGET. Resolve its canonical module version with go list -m github.com/amkargar/gonex, then run go tool gonex upgrade --framework-version CANONICAL_VERSION --dry-run. Review and apply without --dry-run, followed by go mod tidy, tests and contract comparisons.

Upgrade updates the dependency/tool and .gonex.json version metadata. It preserves handwritten code and registries; it does not migrate application code or database schemas. Review the readiness and release gates(/docs/main/production-readiness/) before promoting a candidate.

 Local microservices workflow

Follow First microservice call(/docs/main/microservices-quickstart/) for explicit client profiles and wiring, dev/doctor and independently published contracts. Existing generated paths and TLS defaults are retained. Compatibility(/docs/main/microservices-compatibility/) explains skeleton/example/raw profiles, version coexistence and generation checks.


 Help for every command

sh
gonex -h
gonex build --help
gonex create module -h
gonex help create client


Help is grouped by task. Command-specific help lists only relevant options and
works outside an application without generating files. Color is automatic on
supported terminals and disabled for redirected output, TERM=dumb and
NO_COLOR.

 Build for an operating system and architecture

sh
go tool gonex build --os windows --arch amd64
go tool gonex build --os windows --arch arm64
go tool gonex build --os linux --arch amd64
go tool gonex build --os linux --arch arm64
go tool gonex build --os linux --arch amd64 --out ./release/server


Gonex uses go build -o <file> . underneath. Target options map to GOOS and
GOARCH, defaulting to environment values or the current machine. Supported
pairs are checked against go tool dist list. The default executable is
dist/<os>-<arch>/<app>, with .exe on Windows. Custom relative output paths
resolve from the selected application/service root.

Successful output shows the target and file path; a run command appears only for
native targets. Cross-compilation can require a target C toolchain when a
dependency uses CGO. Compiler diagnostics and failure exit codes remain visible.

title: Framework internals
description: Understand Gonex internals: application registration, transport contracts, adapters, package dependencies and generator ownership.
text:
goNex uses explicit registration and ordinary Go composition. Its business core is independent of HTTP, RPC and persistence adapters.


 Dependency direction

Business services live in modules/NAME/service.go and use plain Go values plus small interfaces owned by the consumer. HTTP adapters own schemas and request mapping; GORM repositories and gRPC clients implement business interfaces at their boundaries. Services should not import Gin, GORM, gRPC, Protobuf or transport DTOs.

mermaid
flowchart LR
    HTTPHTTP adapter --> ServiceBusiness service
    RPCgRPC server adapter --> Service
    Service --> PortLocal dependency interface
    DatabaseGORM repository -. implements .-> Port
    ClientgRPC client adapter -. implements .-> Port


 Registration and lifecycle

A module receives registration capabilities, never ownership of a listener. Registration is explicit, ordered and atomic per App.Register call. The application owns listeners and managed resources. Startup failures close started resources; shutdown drains HTTP and closes resources in reverse order. Stopped applications cannot restart.

Dependencies register before consumers. Context-aware resource lifecycles make background work and cleanup explicit. See modules and lifecycle(/docs/main/modules/).

 HTTP and RPC boundaries

HTTP is unversioned by default. OpenAPI projects the registered typed endpoints. Independent versioned HTTP adapters can share one core service; legacy routes remain unless replacement is explicit.

gRPC is opt-in and has no default listener. Protobuf packages and Go paths carry their API major. Contracts use a separate Go module so services can depend on a shared wire contract without importing each other's business code.

 Generator ownership

Generators own marked registries and record hashes in .gonex.json. They plan and validate writes first, reject handwritten destination collisions and support dry runs. Runtime composition does not scan source or depend on a dependency-injection container.

Independent services have their own Go modules, configuration and migrations. A local go.work file is a development convenience; production dependencies must resolve independently.

 Dependencies

The framework is not dependency-free. The root go.mod declares 10 direct dependencies; indirect dependencies are recorded separately in go.mod and go.sum. Optional integrations share the module dependency graph, but HTTP-only applications need not import or start database/RPC adapters.

| Direct dependency | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| github.com/gin-gonic/gin | HTTP routing and middleware |
| github.com/go-playground/validator/v10 | Typed input validation |
| github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 | Offline OpenAPI schema validation |
| github.com/ncruces/go-sqlite3/gormlite | CGO-free SQLite integration |
| gorm.io/driver/postgres | PostgreSQL driver |
| gorm.io/gorm | Optional persistence adapter |
| google.golang.org/grpc | Optional RPC transport |
| google.golang.org/protobuf | Protobuf runtime and generation support |
| github.com/bufbuild/protocompile | Contract compilation tooling |
| golang.org/x/mod | Go module validation and generator edits |

The list above groups responsibilities; the actual source of truth is go.mod(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/go.mod), including any separate module requirements. Check its first require block when updating the dependency badge.

 Design decisions and limits

Prefer small consumer-owned interfaces and explicit constructors over global registries. Keep validation and the exported contract coherent, rather than silently projecting unsupported DTO behavior. Keep migrations explicit and immutable.

Service discovery is static, cancellation is cooperative and generators do not invent business mappings. See API decisions(/docs/main/api-reference/), upgrade policy(/docs/main/upgrades/) and release scope(/docs/main/release/).

title: Framework development setup
description: Fork and clone Gonex, install its Go toolchain, run the source example and test local framework changes from another app.
text:
Fork and clone

Install Go 1.27.2 and Git. Fork amkargar/gonex(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex) in GitHub, then clone your fork (replace YOUR-USER with your username):

sh
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USER/gonex.git
cd gonex
git remote add upstream https://github.com/amkargar/gonex.git
git switch -c fix/describe-the-change


If you are an upstream maintainer, use the upstream clone and your normal branch workflow. The commands in this contributor section run from the framework repository root, unlike the application guide.

 Resolve dependencies

sh
go mod download
go mod verify


The repository contains several independent Go modules. Resolving the root module alone does not verify the contracts/integration/microservice modules.

 Run the source example

sh
go run ./examples/basic


In another terminal:

sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/users/1


The example's memory-backed response is "id":"1","name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com". Its health, readiness and OpenAPI routes let you inspect lifecycle and typed-contract behavior. This is a framework-development smoke example, not the default setup for a consumer application.

 Build the CLI you are changing

On macOS/Linux:

sh
go build -o gonex ./cmd/gonex
./gonex --help


On Windows, build gonex.exe and invoke it with .\gonex.exe --help. A global previously installed CLI will not automatically use your local changes; run the freshly built executable deliberately.

 Exercise changes from a separate app

Keep a consumer app outside the framework checkout. From the consumer app, use an explicit absolute-path replacement:

sh
go mod edit -replace=github.com/amkargar/gonex=/absolute/path/to/your/gonex
go mod tidy
go test ./...


This helps reproduce behavior through public imports. Remove the replacement and resolve a real dependency before deploying that app. See testing and verification(/docs/main/contribute/testing/) for the framework's own checks.

 Validate microservice developer tooling

The public application tutorial(/docs/main/microservices-quickstart/) is the consumer path. Maintainer tests additionally exercise catalog safety, real child-process trees and an immutable contracts publication fixture on Linux/Windows. See the upstream DX acceptance report(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/microservices-dx/acceptance.md) for exact evidence and unverified independent onboarding.

title: Contribute to Gonex
description: Set up the Gonex framework repository, understand its internals and contribute tested changes to the framework itself.
text:
This section is for developing Gonex itself: its application lifecycle, typed transports, generators, integrations and release tooling.

If you want to build your own API application, start with Build with Gonex(/docs/main/). Installing the package in an application does not require a fork of the framework.

 Contributor path

1. Set up the framework repository(/docs/main/contribute/development-setup/).
2. Read Framework internals(/docs/main/contribute/architecture/) before choosing where a change belongs.
3. Run the relevant tests and checks(/docs/main/contribute/testing/).
4. Prepare a focused pull request(/docs/main/contribute/pull-requests/) with a clear problem and actual verification results.
5. Maintainers use Maintaining releases(/docs/main/contribute/releases/) for release gates and compatibility policy.

 Useful contributions

Bug fixes with reproductions, clearer consumer examples, better error messages, stronger typed-contract validation and focused tests can all be useful. For a larger public API or architectural change, open an issue to discuss the behavior and compatibility implications before committing to an implementation.

The upstream source repository is amkargar/gonex(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex). This documentation website lives separately in amkargar/GoNex-website(https://github.com/amkargar/GoNex-website). Submit framework changes to the former and website/docs presentation changes to the latter.

title: Prepare a contribution
description: Prepare focused Gonex framework pull requests with reproductions, relevant tests, compatible contracts and clear verification notes.
text:
Choose the right repository

Framework behavior, Go APIs, CLI generation and runtime adapters belong in amkargar/gonex(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex). Website navigation, visual design and the consumer/contributor guides belong in amkargar/GoNex-website(https://github.com/amkargar/GoNex-website).

 Describe the problem first

For a bug, include a small reproduction and the expected versus observed behavior. For a feature, explain the application need and compatibility consequences. Discuss broad API changes in an issue before building a large implementation.

 Keep changes focused

- Preserve ordinary Go composition and explicit module registration.
- Keep business-domain examples independent of Gin, GORM or Protobuf where those details belong in adapters.
- Preserve handwritten application code when changing generators.
- Update relevant consumer docs when public behavior changes.
- Treat contract baselines as reviewed compatibility evidence, not files to regenerate merely to silence a failing check.

 Check and review the diff

Run the relevant verification commands(/docs/main/contribute/testing/), inspect generated output and keep unrelated formatting or refactors out of the change. A small, complete change is easier to review than a broad partial implementation.

 Open the pull request

Push your branch to your fork and open a pull request against the intended upstream branch. Explain the user-visible result, the implementation decision that matters to a reviewer, and the checks actually run. Include limitations or skipped platform/database checks. Never include tokens, credentials or local absolute-path overrides.

 Release work is separate

Merging a change does not by itself publish a framework version. Maintainers follow release gates(/docs/main/contribute/releases/) and explicitly review publication.

title: Maintaining releases
description: Review the Gonex maintainer release checklist, compatibility gates, contracts modules and verification requirements.
text:
Current support status

This checkout is not a published release. Local Windows/amd64 verification is recorded in the phase reports. Linux/Windows Go 1.27.2 and latest 1.27 patch are configured CI targets; successful hosted runs are required before claiming that support matrix is verified. Other Go releases and operating systems are unverified. Release builds target Linux, Windows and macOS on amd64/arm64; cross-building alone does not prove runtime support.

 Release checklist

Before a release:

1. Run the test workflow on the release commit: formatting, module verification, tests/vet/build, generated projects, real SQLite, disposable PostgreSQL, Linux race detector, OpenAPI validation/compatibility and benchmark budgets.
2. Run the contracts workflow: pinned official Buf lint/breaking, internal compatibility checks and reproducible official Protobuf generation with a clean generated diff.
3. Review changelog, upgrade instructions, security defaults, examples and all public contract baselines. Baseline updates require review against the previous release, rather than bypassing compatibility checks.
4. Resolve the public repository/module location, choose a semantic tag, and verify generated projects against the resolvable version without local replacements. Publish the independent contracts module under its own module tag when changed.
5. Tag only the reviewed commit. The release workflow reruns reusable test/contracts gates, cross-builds the CLI with an embedded version and uploads checksummed artifacts. It does not publish a GitHub release or push tags.
6. Inspect artifacts and hosted results before separately authorizing publication. Record the actual support matrix and release notes.

 Maintenance and security reports

Only the latest published patch in the active release line is intended to receive fixes; there are no published supported releases yet. Security reports should use a private reporting channel established by the repository owner before publication; do not place credentials or exploit details in public issues. See security configuration(/docs/main/security/).

 Known limits and future scope

Known limits: static service targets, cooperative cancellation, additive migrations without automatic rollback, conservative compatibility checks, no automatic business mapping, no distributed tracing exporter or streaming trace propagation. Brokers, an admin panel and advanced discovery remain future work.

title: Framework testing and verification
description: Run Gonex formatting, unit, contract, integration, race and benchmark checks without confusing framework tests with application tests.
text:
Start with the root module

From the framework repository root:

sh
gofmt -l .
go mod verify
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build ./...


gofmt -l . should print no unformatted files. Use gofmt -w only on the files you intend to change. Add a focused regression test for a behavioral fix, and run the broader checks appropriate to the packages affected.

 Check independent modules

The root go test ./... does not include nested modules. The upstream test workflow also checks:

sh
go -C contracts test ./...
go -C integration/rpc test ./...
go -C integration/rpc vet ./...
go -C integration/rpc build ./...
go -C examples/microservices/services/identity test ./...
go -C examples/microservices/services/orders test ./...


Resolve the relevant modules' dependencies and local-workspace setup before running them. Follow their README files when a service requires additional configuration.

 Typed contracts and generators

sh
go run ./cmd/gonex grpc check
go run ./cmd/gonex openapi validate --file tests/testdata/basic.openapi.json --against tests/testdata/releases/v0.1.0.openapi.json


tests/testdata/releases/v0.1.0.openapi.json is a compatibility fixture, not evidence that a v0.1.0 release is published. Generator changes should preserve handwritten files, reject unsafe paths and have repeatable output.

The contracts workflow also installs the pinned Buf tooling, lints and checks Protobuf compatibility, runs generation and verifies that generated files have no unexplained diff. Inspect the actual contracts workflow(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/.github/workflows/contracts.yml) for its current commands.

 Integration and platform checks

The upstream workflow includes a disposable PostgreSQL service, SQLite integration and a Linux race-detector run. For local race checks on a suitable Go/CGO platform:

sh
go test -race ./...


A test skipped because an external database is unavailable is not a verified database integration. Use the upstream test workflow(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/.github/workflows/test.yml) as the configuration reference, and report skipped or unexecuted checks honestly.

 Benchmark changes carefully

Use paired workloads on the same machine and retain raw output. The upstream benchmark methodology(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/README.md) defines workloads and budgets; small local measurements do not establish production throughput.

 Report actual evidence

In a contribution, list the commands you ran, their outcomes and material checks you could not run. Do not report configured CI targets as passed until the hosted runs succeed.

title: Databases and migrations
description: Use optional GORM adapters with SQLite or PostgreSQL and explicit, checksum-verified SQL migrations.
text:
Configure a database resource

orm.New(orm.OptionsDialect:"sqlite", DSNEnv:"DATABASE_URL") constructs a resource without pinging. Register it with Registrar.Manage; startup opens/pings and shutdown closes its SQL pool. orm.Open(ctx, options) opens immediately for explicit tools/tests. Never log DSNs. Driver errors from opening/pinging are redacted. Pool limits, idle time and lifetime are configurable. The initial verified dialect is real file-backed SQLite using ncruces/gormlite (CGO-free); PostgreSQL uses GORM's official driver.

 Keep repositories at the boundary

Services define local repository interfaces; GORM adapters map values and not-found/unique errors. orm.Transaction accepts a GORM callback only at the adapter boundary. A service needing atomic multi-write behavior should define a small local transaction callback interface implemented by that adapter.

 Apply immutable migrations

Migrations are immutable UTF-8 SQL files named 000001_description.up.sql. Use migration.New(pool, dialect, files) with an embedded or directory fs.FS, then explicitly call Up(ctx) or Status(ctx). SQL must be transaction-compatible; do not put BEGIN/COMMIT, nontransactional DDL or connection-level PRAGMAs inside a migration. The runner uses one transaction for the full pending batch, a version/checksum history table, SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE via serializable isolation, and PostgreSQL transaction advisory locks. Concurrent runners cannot apply the same migration twice. Changes to applied contents/names, missing versions and out-of-order history fail clearly. Repeating an unchanged migration set is a no-op. Status initializes an empty history table if needed.

No AutoMigrate or implicit application-start schema changes. Down migrations are deliberately absent from the example because dropping persisted users is destructive. Forward corrections use new versions.

 Add persistence to your application

From your generated application root:

sh
go tool gonex create module messages --db
go mod tidy


Configure SQLite in the process environment. POSIX shell:

sh
export DATABASE_DIALECT=sqlite
export DATABASE_URL='file:app.db?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)'
go tool gonex db migrate
go tool gonex run


PowerShell:

powershell
$env:DATABASE_DIALECT='sqlite'
$env:DATABASE_URL='file:app.db?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)'
go tool gonex db migrate
go tool gonex run


The starter GET /messages reads its seeded message from the database. Extend its handwritten service, repository, schemas and routes for your domain; --db does not generate a complete model CRUD API. Serving never runs migrations automatically. No framework checkout or automatic .env loading is required.

 Verify database behavior

Framework maintainers run go test ./... in the framework repository to test file-backed SQLite CRUD, transactions, migration rollback/checksums/concurrency and lifecycle cleanup. PostgreSQL integration is explicitly skipped unless GONEX_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN identifies an empty disposable test database; it is never inferred from production DATABASE_URL. PostgreSQL credentials and deployment-specific behavior require that integration environment.

title: Debug mode and development pages
description: Use DEBUG=true for the Gonex duck welcome page and browser error diagnostics, while keeping JSON API contracts and production responses unchanged.
text:
Debug pages are opt-in and disabled by default.

 Configure a generated application

Set these environment variables in the process running your application:

sh
 Linux / macOS
DEBUG=true go tool gonex run


powershell
 PowerShell
$env:DEBUG = "true"
go tool gonex run

 Turn debugging off
$env:DEBUG = "false"


The generated config.Load() maps the literal DEBUG=true to
config.Config.Debug. Unset, false and other values disable debugging.
The core library stays explicit: manual applications set config.ConfigDebug: true.
Environment variables are read by the generated app, not automatically by the
library. A .env.example is a reference; Gonex does not automatically load it.

 Existing applications

Upgrading Gonex preserves handwritten configuration files. If your app was created
before this feature, first update its Gonex dependency, then add the environment
mapping to the config.Config value returned by your own config.Load():

go
Debug: os.Getenv("DEBUG") == "true",


This is a field inside the existing configuration literal. Keep the other fields
and the existing os import. Restart the application after setting the environment
variable.

 Welcome page

With DEBUG=true, visiting GET / shows Welcome to Gonex, the Gonex duck,
and links to the website and documentation. The image is embedded in the
executable, so this page works offline and does not require a static directory.
An OpenAPI link appears only when OpenAPI is enabled.

Your own matching route always wins, including a custom root or catch-all route.
With DEBUG=false, Gonex does not install the welcome page or debug image.
Normal application routes continue to work.

 Browser error pages

A browser request accepting text/html receives an HTML development page for
uncommitted error responses, including:

- 404: request path and registered routes.
- 405: a method that is not supported by a registered route.
- Binding/validation errors: status and validation information.
- Returned handler errors: original error message, type and stack.
- Panics: panic value and stack trace.

The page includes method, query-free path, matched route and request ID. HTML is
escaped. Request bodies, headers, cookies, query strings and environment
variables are not dumped. Error strings and stacks can contain sensitive details,
so keep DEBUG=false on public deployments.

Requests for JSON (or without an explicit HTML preference) keep their normal API
response shape and generic internal errors, even with debug enabled.
This preserves typed OpenAPI contracts for API clients.

Already committed responses, streams, hijacked connections and error responses
over 64 KiB are not rewritten. Successful responses and streams pass through
immediately. Debug HTML is never cached and contains no external scripts.

 Disable debugging in production

sh
DEBUG=false
GONEX_ENV=production


GONEX_ENV controls logging defaults; it does not implicitly turn debug on or off.
The two switches remain explicit. Restart the application after changing them.

title: Deploy your application
description: Build and host a Gonex JSON API as a Go service, with explicit configuration, readiness and frontend hosting.
text:
A Gonex app needs a backend runtime

Gonex is a Go backend. Its compiled executable must run on a server, container platform or other host that supports a long-running Go process. GitHub Pages serves static files and cannot execute that backend.

If you use a static Nuxt/Vue frontend, you can host it on Pages while the Gonex API runs elsewhere. See frontend integration(/docs/main/frontend/) for the boundary.

 Build the application

From your application module:

sh
go mod tidy
go test ./...
go tool gonex build --os linux --arch amd64
 Output: dist/linux-amd64/shop


Deploy the compiled API binary and its explicit runtime configuration. Frontend assets are built and hosted separately.

 Configure the listening address

The tutorial programs read HTTP_ADDRESS and pass it to config.Config. For a platform that expects a listener on all interfaces, configure the address in the process environment before starting the application:

sh
DEBUG=false GONEX_ENV=production HTTP_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0:8080 ./dist/linux-amd64/shop


This is POSIX shell syntax. On PowerShell, set $env:GONEX_ENV = 'production' and $env:HTTP_ADDRESS = '0.0.0.0:8080', also set $env:DEBUG = 'false', then start the Windows executable built for the server architecture. Bind only to interfaces appropriate for your deployment; use 127.0.0.1:8080 when a local reverse proxy should be the only entry point.

Gonex does not automatically load .env files. Your executable or process manager owns environment/configuration loading. The default config.Config listener is loopback-only.

 Configure HTTPS and frontend routing

Terminate HTTPS with your platform or reverse proxy. For a separate frontend on the same origin, serve the frontend at / and forward /api/ to the Gonex listener while preserving its /api prefix. For a different-origin frontend, configure the backend's allowed CORS origin and the frontend's public API URL.

Decide whether /openapi.json should be public. Set DisableOpenAPI in the application configuration when it should not be exposed. For generated CLI applications, use their documented GONEX_DISABLE_OPENAPI option.

 Production logs

Set GONEX_ENV=production in the generated application to select JSON logs by default. Collect stderr through your platform; configure level/format using the logging guide(/docs/main/logging/). The localhost startup URL is a local convenience, not your public HTTPS origin.

 Health, readiness and shutdown

- Use /healthz for the lightweight health response.
- Use /readyz for application/dependency readiness.
- Send a normal termination signal and allow the configured shutdown budget to drain work.
- Make managed resources honor context cancellation.

Review operations(/docs/main/operations/) for readiness and resource lifecycles. Apply security configuration(/docs/main/security/) before exposing the app.

 Databases and version pinning

Run explicit migrations before starting the application. Set the database environment expected by your executable; serving does not automatically migrate schemas. Do not deploy a go.mod that points to a developer machine's absolute replacement path. Keep the reviewed framework version in go.mod / go.sum, and review upgrade compatibility(/docs/main/upgrades/) before changing it.

 Current release status

The documentation snapshot has no published stable release. Source availability and successful local examples do not establish a production support guarantee. Review the release status(/docs/main/release/) and verify your deployment environment.


 Disable development pages

Set DEBUG=false explicitly. Debug mode defaults off but can expose original errors and stack traces when enabled. It is independent of GONEX_ENV. The welcome page and embedded duck are unavailable when debug is off. See debug mode(/docs/main/debug/).

title: Connect a frontend
description: Use Gonex as the backend for a Nuxt, Vue, React or Flutter frontend, with clear API URLs and deployment boundaries.
text: Gonex handles backend HTTP APIs. Nuxt, Vue, React or Flutter can consume those APIs. They do not import Go packages directly: the browser/client communicates with your Go process over HTTP. Start with a working endpoint Complete Build a REST API(/docs/main/building-api/) and confirm that http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/users returns a JSON list after completing the resource API guide. Keep that Gonex process running while developing your frontend. Choose how the frontend is served | Approach | What serves the page? | Where Gonex runs | | --- | --- | --- | | Separate Nuxt/Vue/React frontend | Its dev server, static host or SSR server | A Go backend process | | Static frontend hosted on GitHub Pages | GitHub Pages | A separate backend host | Browser requests on the same origin If a reverse proxy routes /api/ to Gonex and serves your frontend on the same HTTPS origin, use relative requests: ts const response = await fetch('/api/users') if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Could not load users') const data: items: id: string; name: string; email: string = await response.json() console.log(data.items) Configure the reverse proxy to forward /api/users without stripping /api, because that is the route registered by the resource API example. In development, use your frontend tool's development proxy if you want the same relative URLs. Nuxt example with an explicit API origin The following client-only request can be placed inside a Nuxt page's Set NUXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE to your backend's public HTTPS origin in production. For a statically generated frontend, configure it at build time and rebuild when it changes. An end user's browser cannot use your development machine's 127.0.0.1 as a production backend. Different origins require a CORS policy A frontend at http://localhost:3000 and a backend at http://127.0.0.1:8080 are different origins. The browser blocks cross-origin calls unless the backend explicitly permits the frontend origin. A development proxy avoids this browser cross-origin boundary; a separately hosted frontend needs a deliberate CORS policy. The example API does not enable CORS automatically. Configure it according to the security guide(/docs/main/security/). CORS is not authentication. Avoid broad origin/credential policies; keep secrets on the backend. If using cookie-authenticated cross-site requests, review cookie and CSRF behavior as part of your application security design. Static hosting is only the frontend GitHub Pages can host a generated frontend, but cannot run your Gonex server or database. Deploy the API to a host that runs Go services, then configure the frontend's API URL and allowed origin. See deployment(/docs/main/deployment/).

title: gRPC and contracts
description: Configure optional Gonex gRPC servers and clients, versioned Protobuf contracts, deadlines, TLS and mTLS.
text:
Opt in to gRPC

Import github.com/amkargar/gonex/grpc only in transport/bootstrap code. HTTP-only modules do not import it or start gRPC listeners. config.ConfigDisableHTTP:true permits a gRPC-only process. Manage servers and client pools with Registrar.Manage so failed startup/shutdown releases them. Resources exposing Errors() also report asynchronous failures to App.Run.

 Register a server

grpc.NewServer(ServerOptionsAddress:...,TLS:...) constructs without binding. Supply generated registration callbacks through Server.Register, then let the app Start/Close it. The built-in standard gRPC health service reports serving status. Application services must not import gRPC or generated messages; map at server/client boundaries using ToStatus/FromStatus. Unknown errors are redacted.

 Configure TLS and mTLS

TLS is required by default. Load a server certificate and trust roots using crypto/tls and crypto/x509. mTLS uses RequireAndVerifyClientCert plus ClientCAs; the client supplies its certificate. Client InsecureSkipVerify is rejected. Only explicit DevelopmentInsecure permits plaintext for local development. Keep caller-provided TLS certificate/key material immutable after configuration.

 Reuse managed clients

Create one immutable ClientConfig per target/security/transport setup with NewClientConfig. Reuse that config with a shared Clients manager to reuse a connection concurrently. Different immutable configs never share a connection, even when targets are equal; this avoids credential/identity/dialer mixing. grpc.Client(pool, config, generated.NewServiceClient) returns a typed generated client. Creation is lazy; pool.Ready(ctx,config) separately proves connectivity and requires a bounded caller context. Registry resolves explicit service names to configs. No write retry policy is installed; configured retry policies are disabled.

 Set deadlines and drain requests

Default unary and stream RPC timeouts are five seconds, configurable per server/client; shorter incoming contexts win. Stream timeouts bound the whole stream lifetime. Handlers must honor their contexts. Server.Close uses graceful stop, then force-stop if the supplied context expires. App.Run supplies its configured shutdown timeout.

 Generate versioned contracts

Contracts are a separate Go module at contracts/. All packages and Go paths are versioned. gonex grpc generate compiles with pinned Buf protocompile v0.14.1 and invokes official protoc-gen-go v1.36.10 / protoc-gen-go-grpc v1.6.0. This Go-only compiler is the one used by Buf; protoc installation is unnecessary. --dry-run compiles/checks without plugins or writes. Generated files are staged; sources and handwritten adapters are preserved. Network/cache access is needed to obtain pinned tools on first use.

 Check compatibility

schema.binpb is the generated descriptor set. baseline.binpb is the explicitly frozen initial release contract. gonex grpc check rejects removed/changed files, messages, fields, enum values and RPC signatures, allowing additions. Generation enforces this baseline too. This conservative checker may require a new major for option-only changes; CI also runs Buf FILE compatibility against the same descriptor baseline. Update baselines only during a reviewed release, never to suppress a failed compatibility gate. buf.yaml and buf.gen.yaml support a standard external Buf toolchain as well.

 Verify your application's contracts

From your generated app or workspace, use go tool gonex grpc generate, go tool gonex grpc check and go tool gonex check. Test your own provider/consumer mapping and failure behavior. Framework TLS integration fixtures are documented separately in Contribute: testing(/docs/main/contribute/testing/).

 Recovery and observability

Unary and stream recovery returns redacted Internal errors. grpc.ServerTLS and grpc.ClientTLS load verified certificate configurations with redacted file errors. The optional observability/grpc unary interceptors propagate traceparent and collect fixed-method metrics; see operations(/docs/main/operations/). Application readiness can check managed server lifecycle and explicitly registered downstream client connectivity.

 Additional Buf checks

Your contracts module includes buf.yaml and buf.gen.yaml for an external Buf workflow. Add Buf lint and compatibility checks to your application's CI when needed. Framework maintainers' pinned tool installer and release gates belong in contributor testing(/docs/main/contribute/testing/).

 Local microservices workflow

Follow First microservice call(/docs/main/microservices-quickstart/) for explicit client profiles and wiring, dev/doctor and independently published contracts. Existing generated paths and TLS defaults are retained. Compatibility(/docs/main/microservices-compatibility/) explains skeleton/example/raw profiles, version coexistence and generation checks.

title: HTTP and OpenAPI
description: Build typed HTTP endpoints with Gin adapters, request validation and OpenAPI 3.1 contracts in Gonex.
text:
Register typed endpoints

Declare routes together and pass typed handler methods directly. Request and response types are inferred from each handler:

go
func Register(r transport.EndpointRegistrar, actions Actions) error 
    h := HandlerActions: actions
    return transport.Routes(r,
        transport.Post("/users", h.Create).Name("createUser").Errors(409),
        transport.Get("/users/:id", h.Get).Name("getUser").Errors(404),
    )



Import transport "github.com/amkargar/gonex/http". A handler has the signature func(context.Context, Request) (Response, error); named structs in schemas.go declare the contract. Give every route a unique .Name(...) for its OpenAPI operation ID.

Get, Put, Patch, Head and Options default to 200; Post defaults to 201 and Delete to 204. Override with .Status(...). A 204 endpoint should return NoBody.

Optional metadata stays next to the route: .Summary(...), .Description(...), .Tags(...), .Errors(...), .Use(...), .Security(requirements, schemes), .MaxBodyBytes(...) and .Examples(request, response). Middleware runs before binding and validation. Versioned registrars work with the same route declarations.

Routes uses the existing typed registration pipeline: validation, binding, request limits, error mapping and OpenAPI remain identical. Return its error from Module.Register; the application commits module registration only after all modules succeed. Reusing a declaration to register multiple paths is discouraged; define each route once during startup.

The lower-level http.Register(registrar, http.EndpointRequest, Response...) API remains supported for existing applications. Business services return plain Go values; adapters map those into transport schemas.


 Bind and validate requests

Each request wrapper field declares exactly one origin: path:"id", query:"page", header:"X-Token" or body:"true". There may be only one body field. Parameters are scalar or pointers to scalars. Path placeholders must match field bindings. Body schemas use standard json tags and validate tags. Required, min/max, email, nested structs and slice dive validation are supported. Use pointers to distinguish absent numeric/boolean values from zero/false; required on a pointer requires presence, while required on a scalar rejects its zero value.

| Origin | Example tag | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Path | path:"id" | Required; must match the route placeholder |
| Query | query:"page" | Scalar or pointer to a scalar |
| Header | header:"X-Token" | Scalar or pointer; duplicates are rejected |
| Body | body:"true" | One JSON body field per request wrapper |

 Handle failures and limits

Malformed JSON, missing required parameters and unsupported content types return 400. Unknown or incorrectly cased JSON fields, duplicate object keys, trailing values, duplicate query/header values and null nonnullable bodies are rejected. Validation failures return 422 with field paths and codes. Request bodies default to 1 MiB; set MaxBodyBytes per endpoint. Application errors must be declared in Errors to expose their mapped status/message; undeclared/internal errors return a redacted 500. Context deadline failures return a documented 504. 204 responses have no body.

 Describe endpoint metadata

Optional summary, description, tags, request/response examples, security requirements/schemes and middleware live on the same endpoint contract. Middleware must return documented response shapes/statuses. Low-level Registrar.Handle is an escape hatch for raw Gin routes and is not projected into OpenAPI; public application endpoints should use typed registration.

 Serve and export documents

/openapi.json is enabled by default; DisableOpenAPI removes it in production. /docs is an opt-in local document link (DocsEnabled), without externally loaded assets. Runtime-owned paths reject conflicts. The specification is built and validated once during startup, not per request. App.OpenAPI() explicitly exports without starting a listener.

 Supported DTO schemas

Schemas support named/nested/recursive structs, pointers/nullability, string-keyed maps and slices; component names include a stable package hash. Input requiredness follows validation, output requiredness follows JSON omission. Nested input objects require pointers (except time.Time) so presence has an explicit representation. A value body wrapper is already required: omit its redundant required validation tag. Anonymous embedded fields, byte slices, non-string map keys, custom JSON encodings and unsupported JSON tag options require explicit DTOs. Supported validation tags are required, omitempty, min, max, email, dive and -; unsupported or contradictory constraints fail registration. The official OpenAPI Initiative 3.1 schema is vendored with its source URL; santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema v6 validates generated documents offline.

 Freeze and compare contracts

Contracts and handler slices are detached from caller-owned metadata at registration. Security requirements must reference declared schemes. Export a version with gonex openapi generate --http-version v1 --out v1.json; compare it with a released baseline using gonex openapi validate --file v1.json --against baseline.json. Compatibility checking is conservative; see upgrade policy(/docs/main/upgrades/).


 Browser diagnostics

With DEBUG=true, requests accepting HTML receive a development error page for uncommitted error responses. JSON clients retain their typed API contracts. See debug mode(/docs/main/debug/) for the welcome page, exception details and production settings.

title: Build APIs with Gonex
description: Install Gonex, generate projects and modules with its CLI, and develop typed JSON APIs with validation, OpenAPI and structured logs.
text:
Gonex is an API-first Go framework with explicit modules, typed request/response schemas, validation and OpenAPI. Install the dependency, create your own application, add modules and implement APIs inside that application.

 Start building

1. Install Gonex and its CLI(/docs/main/installation/).
2. Create a project, add a module and run it(/docs/main/quick-start/).
3. Build a REST API(/docs/main/building-api/) with create/list/get endpoints.
4. Understand the generated structure(/docs/main/project-structure/).
5. Enable the welcome page and development errors(/docs/main/debug/).
6. Configure server output and logs(/docs/main/logging/), then deploy(/docs/main/deployment/).

A database, gRPC and HTTP versioning are optional. Frontends consume Gonex over HTTP; the built-in welcome and error pages are development diagnostics, while frontends remain separate applications.

 Familiar API responsibilities

| Responsibility | Gonex file |
| --- | --- |
| Request/response schemas and validation, DTOs and validation | schemas.go |
| HTTP handlers, request-to-service mapping | handlers.go |
| Endpoint registration, typed route declarations | routes.go |
| Business behavior | service.go |
| Feature composition | module.go |

The comparison describes responsibilities, not identical APIs. Automatic model-to-CRUD generation and an administration interface are not current features.

 Two documentation paths

Build with Gonex is the main track for application developers: package installation, CLI projects, modules, API development, optional persistence and deployment. No framework fork or clone is required.

Contribute to Gonex(/docs/main/contribute/) is for changing the framework itself: source setup, internals, tests and pull requests. Clone instructions stay there.

 Version support

The version selector chooses a documentation snapshot. It is separate from optional HTTP API versions such as /api/v1. These guides pin a reviewed main development snapshot; no stable release is assumed. See release status(/docs/main/release/) and upgrades(/docs/main/upgrades/).

title: Install Gonex and its CLI
description: Install Gonex as a Go library and project-local development tool, then generate an API application without cloning the framework.
text:
Requirements

Use Go 1.27.2 and a configured Go module proxy or dependency cache. Gonex is installed into your own project; you do not clone the framework to build an API. There is no published release yet: these commands pin the reviewed development commit 3ca54b46cb42.

 Install the bootstrap CLI

sh
go install github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@3ca54b46cb42
gonex --version


Ensure Go's binary directory is on PATH: GOBIN, or GOPATH/bin when GOBIN is unset. go env GOBIN GOPATH prints those locations. On Windows the executable is gonex.exe. If your shell cannot find it, add the installation directory to PATH and reopen the shell.

 Generate your own application

sh
gonex new shop --module example.com/acme/shop
cd shop
go mod tidy
go tool gonex create module users
go tool gonex run


Choose your application's Go module path. The installed CLI uses its actual module version as the generated framework dependency, including pseudo-versions. No unpublished default release is assumed. A locally built CLI must receive an explicit valid --framework-version VERSION.

 Project-local development tool

The generated go.mod includes both a Gonex requirement and:

go
tool github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex


Continue with go tool gonex inside the application. Go selects the project's CLI version, avoiding accidental use of another global CLI. This is a development tool dependency tracked in go.mod/go.sum; it does not link the CLI into your server binary. Framework and CLI share one module version. See Go tool dependencies(https://go.dev/doc/modules/managing-dependencies).

 Add the library to an existing application

From the existing module root:

sh
go get github.com/amkargar/gonex@3ca54b46cb42


Add your Gonex imports and explicit application/module composition, then run go mod tidy. Installing a dependency does not replace an existing HTTP server automatically. You can also track the CLI in an existing Go module:

sh
go get -tool github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@3ca54b46cb42


The minimum Go patch and dependency versions include security fixes. Use the reviewed snapshot rather than an older development commit, and consult production readiness(/docs/main/production-readiness/) for the current release decision.

 Check the selected dependency

sh
go list -m github.com/amkargar/gonex
go tool gonex --version


Use actual published tags once available, or reviewed commits while the framework is in development. Keep go.mod and go.sum with your application. Go resolves commit references into canonical pseudo-versions.

Continue with Quick start(/docs/main/quick-start/). Framework checkout/replacement instructions belong only in Contribute(/docs/main/contribute/development-setup/).

title: Server output and logging
description: Configure readable server startup URLs, correlated request logs, log levels and structured production JSON in a Gonex application.
text:
Gonex uses application-scoped log/slog loggers for lifecycle and HTTP completion events. It does not replace the process-wide default logger.

 Run an application

From a CLI-generated app:

sh
go tool gonex run


Readable development output shows the application name, resolved Gonex version, environment, listening address and clickable local URL. Wildcard listeners (0.0.0.0 or ::) display a localhost URL with the actual port; this is a local convenience, not a public deployment URL. OpenAPI and optional /docs URLs are shown only when enabled, along with registered version-specific documents. HTTP-disabled apps show no HTTP URLs. The startup event is emitted after resources start and the listener binds, never on a failed bind; dependency readiness is still reported separately by /readyz.

Ctrl+C triggers graceful shutdown in the generated executable. Lifecycle events report startup failure, stopping, shutdown failure and successful stop.

 Configuration

The generated config.Load() reads these variables:

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| APP_NAME | Gonex | Application name in startup output |
| GONEX_ENV | development | production selects JSON for the auto format |
| GONEX_LOG_LEVEL | INFO | DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR |
| GONEX_LOG_FORMAT | auto | auto, pretty, text, json |
| GONEX_LOG_COLOR | auto | Pretty output: auto, always, never |

Auto color is disabled when stderr is not a terminal, TERM=dumb, or NO_COLOR is set. JSON is one object per line. Logs go to stderr, suitable for container/platform log collection. This does not implement file rotation, remote storage or an external collector. Environment variables are read by the generated app configuration, not implicitly by the core library. Export them in your process environment; .env is not loaded automatically.

Manual consumers configure config.Config with Name, Environment, LogLevel, LogFormat and LogColor. A caller-supplied Logger slog.Logger takes precedence. DisableRequestLogging and DisableStartupBanner opt out of completion events and the startup summary respectively.

 Request events

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| time, level, msg | slog timestamp, severity and event message |
| service, environment | Application identity and environment from config |
| trace_id | W3C trace identifier shared with unary RPC calls |
| request_id | Fresh server-generated identifier, also returned as X-Request-ID |
| method, path | Standard HTTP method (other tokens use OTHER) and registered route pattern; unknown paths use unmatched |
| status, duration_ms | Response status and elapsed processing milliseconds |
| error | Safe framework error code or handler panic, when applicable |

Successful responses use INFO; 4xx use WARN; 5xx and panics use ERROR. One completion event is emitted per request, including recovered panics. Additional business log events are separate. Filtering by log level may suppress lower-severity events. Existing metrics/trace middleware can still be installed separately.

The default request event excludes request/response bodies, headers, query strings, raw path parameter values, arbitrary error strings and panic payloads. Application code remains responsible for the fields it explicitly logs.

 Log from a service

go
observability.Logger(ctx, nil).InfoContext(ctx,
    "user created",
    "module", "users",
    "user_id", user.ID,
)


Import github.com/amkargar/gonex/observability. Pass the request context into services; the logger carries its request ID. Outside an HTTP request, supply the application logger as the fallback (observability.Logger(ctx, application.Logger())). The module field is explicit business context, not inferred from the URL. observability.RequestID(ctx) reads the current ID directly.

For a custom destination, construct a logger with observability.NewLogger(observability.LogOptionsOutput: writer, Format: "json", Level: "INFO") and pass it through config.Config.Logger. Keep asynchronous tasks' cancellation and log context deliberate.

Lifecycle failures use safe startup_failed/resource_failed/shutdown_failed codes in default logs. Detailed causes are returned to the caller for deliberate private handling; do not log credential-bearing causes indiscriminately.


 Read the server summary

The development output groups the application name, local URL, actual listening
address, OpenAPI URL, environment, framework version and debug flag. Request
lines align method, route, status and elapsed milliseconds, while retaining
correlation IDs. Production auto mode continues to use JSON.

For the browser welcome page and detailed errors, see DEBUG configuration(/docs/main/debug/).

title: Microservice compatibility
description: Understand catalog ownership, safe client generation, contract versions and independent Go module deployment.
text:
Existing main.go/config/modules paths remain supported. No new cmd/server/internal/bootstrap profile or automatic path migration is introduced. Re-generation refuses caller-owned destinations before writes; dry-run changes no project files and runs no codegen plugins.

New schema-1 gonex.yaml is caller-editable local configuration. It rejects unknown/duplicate keys, duplicate listener ports, path escape, symlink service paths and non-loopback endpoints. It does not replace go.mod versions or business bootstrap. Declared dependency cycles warn rather than banning peer topology. Older workspaces retain run/build/check without a catalog; add a validated catalog to opt into dev/doctor.

Existing create service NAME retains HTTP defaults; explicit --http, --grpc, both, or --transport none select listeners. Module adapters are separate; HTTP API versions remain opt-in. Conflicting/irrelevant flags are rejected before writes.

New clients default to compile-time skeletons. This deliberately exposes unfinished mapping/wiring. --profile raw retains the previous typed-client/manual-bootstrap workflow; existing client files are never rewritten. --profile example is limited to the exact descriptor-verified demonstration contract, with --rpc Service.Method resolving ambiguity.

v1 keeps its previous names. v2 gets separate files/settings/types. Share a managed pool/config explicitly using generated WithConfig constructors when multiple versions/modules consume one target; do not call multiple convenience helpers for the same security profile. No global singleton or locator exists.

Edit contracts/proto; pb.go is generated. grpc generate stages outputs atomically, protects handwritten destinations and checks baseline.binpb when supplied. grpc generate --check regenerates in memory and reports drift without project writes. A placeholder v0.1.0 is not a released baseline; published baselines remain deliberate inputs. Buf/Go API gates stay enabled.

Publish actual contracts through normal module hosting or an immutable proxy before isolated deployment. Services build with GOWORK=off and no replacement. CI's disposable file proxy proves that mechanism; it is not a public release or required runtime infrastructure.

Existing bounded RPC deadlines, TLS/mTLS, health/readiness, drain and disabled automatic retries remain intact. Operators, meshes, dynamic discovery, the optional graph command and new path-template profiles are deferred.

title: First microservice call
description: Install Gonex, wire Orders to Identity explicitly and run local services with a single supervised command.
text:
Use a supported patched Go toolchain (minimum 1.27.2). A monolith remains simpler: use gonex new shop --module YOUR_MODULE unless you need independent services. This tutorial installs Gonex as a library/tool; do not clone the framework.

 Create the workspace

Install a reviewed CLI version (@main is a development snapshot, not a stable release). Replace example.com/acme/commerce with the Go module prefix you own before publishing contracts.

sh
go install github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@main
gonex new commerce --module example.com/acme/commerce --arch microservices
cd commerce
go mod tidy
go tool gonex create service identity --grpc
go tool gonex create service orders --http
go tool gonex create module users --service identity --transport grpc --version v1
go tool gonex create module orders --service orders --transport http
go tool gonex create client identity --service orders --module orders --version v1 --profile example --rpc UsersService.GetUsersMessage


There are seven creation commands, one explicit dependency-preparation step and one run command. Compilation/download time is environment dependent; an independent five-minute onboarding result has not been measured.

The example profile is deliberately limited to the descriptor-verified empty-request/string-message contract just generated. It maps the selected RPC response to a plain string. It does not infer a real user/order schema. For your own contract use the default skeleton profile, implement your local interface/field/error mapping, then remove its explicit GONEX_TODO_... compile-time marker. doctor reports its file. raw retains the old typed-client-only workflow for advanced manual wiring.

 Make the two user-owned business edits

Replace services/orders/modules/orders/service.go with:

go
package orders

import "context"

type IdentityReader interface 
    Message(context.Context) (string, error)


type Service struct  identity IdentityReader 

func NewService(identity IdentityReader) Service 
    return &Serviceidentity: identity


func (s Service) Message(ctx context.Context) (string, error) 
    return s.identity.Message(ctx)



This file has no Protobuf or framework imports. Replace only NewModuleService in services/orders/modules/orders/module.go with:

go
func NewModuleService(r app.Registrar) (Service, error) 
    client, err := NewIdentityForModule(r)
    if err != nil  return nil, err 
    return NewService(client), nil



The generated helper creates one managed pool/config for this target, constructs the exact typed client, registers connection readiness and cleans up on helper failure. It does not choose your domain interface or alter your handwritten factory. Call it once in that factory. For multiple modules/versions, own the service bootstrap explicitly: share a managed rpc.NewClients pool and rpc.NewClientConfig, then use the generated NewIdentityClientWithConfig/NewIdentityV2ClientWithConfig constructors. Do not call multiple convenience helpers for the same target/security profile.

In services/orders/modules/orders/http/routes.go, add Errors: int503, 504, to the Endpoint literal, so the API explicitly declares provider-unavailable responses. Adapt the generated service_test.go to the constructor you now own (inject a fake IdentityReader); the generator does not rewrite that test. These are application edits; no framework-owned registry needs manual changes.

 Run locally

The explicit root go mod tidy above prepares the CLI/framework dependencies. The generated go.work resolves local contracts source for the initial build. New services do not require a fictional contracts release, so no publication is needed for this first run. Service-level go mod tidy requires an actual published contracts version because tidy resolves that module independently of go.work. Prepare the root CLI module for initial local builds. Publication and isolated builds are a separate, explicit step below.

sh
go tool gonex doctor --dev-insecure
go tool gonex dev --dev-insecure


--dev-insecure prominently enables local loopback plaintext only. The runner refuses it with GONEX_ENV=production and refuses contradictory TLS/insecure settings. No flag is persisted to production templates. Without it, configure server GRPC_TLS_CERT/GRPC_TLS_KEY and client CLIENTS_IDENTITY_CA/SERVER_NAME (plus client certificates when using mTLS). No credentials belong in gonex.yaml and no .env file is loaded automatically.

The console prefixes each service's output and prints configured HTTP/gRPC addresses. Open the Orders address shown by doctor (http://127.0.0.1:8081/orders in this fresh tutorial). The response is "message":"users". Configured addresses are not readiness assertions; use /readyz and application logs. Ctrl+C stops all owned services. An unexpected child exit stops its siblings and returns a non-zero result.
