dev --service orders selects only Orders; it does not silently start Identity. Start its provider separately or it will become unready/return a bounded 503. Readiness is connection readiness, not a promise that every business RPC is healthy. Mutating RPCs are never retried automatically.

 Choose transports and override local addresses

- create service NAME --http: HTTP-only listener.
- create service NAME --grpc: gRPC-only listener, including the managed health server.
- create service NAME --http --grpc: both listeners.
- create service NAME --transport none: worker with no listener.
- Existing create service NAME keeps its HTTP default. Module adapters and service listeners are distinct; changing a listener later requires an explicit catalog/configuration change, not editing a generated registry.

The caller-editable gonex.yaml owns only local service paths/addresses/declared client edges. .gonex.json owns generator metadata; go.mod owns dependency versions. The existing main.go/config/modules layout is preserved.

Use GONEX_SERVICES_IDENTITY_GRPC_ADDRESS or GONEX_SERVICES_ORDERS_HTTP_ADDRESS to override individual listeners. Provider overrides flow to declared local clients unless CLIENTS_IDENTITY_ADDRESS explicitly overrides the target. Shared HTTP_ADDRESS/GRPC_ADDRESS is accepted only when selecting one service; it is ambiguous for a multi-service run. The local catalog rejects non-loopback addresses; production deployment addresses belong to your normal per-process environment/configuration.

 Publish contracts and deploy independently

New generators do not insert an unpublished contracts requirement. Older templates may contain a v0.1.0 placeholder; it is not a released Gonex contract. Publish contracts as a real Go module using your own repository/subdirectory tags or an immutable Go module proxy. Set the actual published version in each consuming service's go.mod, then explicitly tidy/test/build each service with GOWORK=off. Deployment must not use a local replace or require the workspace.

sh
 Run inside each consuming service, after publishing the actual contract version.
go get YOUR_CONTRACTS_MODULE@PUBLISHED_VERSION
go mod tidy
go test ./...
go build ./...


Set GOWORK=off in the shell for those commands (PowerShell: $env:GOWORK='off'). For an already prepared local catalog, gonex dev --isolated also uses GOWORK=off. Its builds disable module proxy/network tool downloads, use -mod=readonly and require the chosen toolchain/dependencies to be installed beforehand. Go's normal build cache and local workspace checksum file may be populated; no silent tidy is performed.

CI rehearses this supported publication mechanism by publishing an immutable contracts zip/mod/info fixture to a disposable file proxy, checking its SHA256, then resolving independent service modules without replacements/workspace resolution. That fixture is not a public stable release. The same installed public CLI and mapped tutorial are checked on Linux/Windows.

See compatibility(/docs/main/microservices-compatibility/), troubleshooting(/docs/main/microservices-troubleshooting/) and acceptance(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/microservices-dx/acceptance.md) for exact scope and evidence.

title: Microservice diagnostics
description: Resolve local ports, TLS, contract generation, unfinished mapping and supervised process failures.
text:
| Diagnostic | Action |
| --- | --- |
| mapping_todo / GONEX_TODO | Implement the local interface, descriptor-to-domain field/error mapping and factory injection. Remove the compile-time marker deliberately. |
| wiring_missing | Call NewProviderForModule once from the caller-owned factory. Static analysis is guidance; test the actual mapped RPC. Raw clients use manual bootstrap. |
| server_tls_missing / client_tls_missing | Supply TLS material or explicitly select --dev-insecure for loopback development. No production plaintext default is generated. |
| invalid_server_tls / invalid_client_tls | Verify certificate, key, CA, server name and expiration. Doctor parses material; a live handshake validates identity/connectivity. Credential contents/raw loader errors are never printed. |
| security_flags_conflict | Unset insecure flags when TLS material is configured. |
| production_plaintext | Remove development insecurity; GONEX_ENV=production cannot use it through dev. |
| port_unavailable | Stop the conflicting process or change the service-scoped address/catalog. The runner never kills unrelated processes. Check/start bind races remain possible and child failure is reported. |
| Shared listener address is ambiguous | Use GONEX_SERVICES_NAME_HTTP_ADDRESS/GRPC_ADDRESS or select one --service. |
| contracts_stale / contracts_not_generated | Explicitly run grpc generate or dev --generate. grpc generate --check checks artifact drift without project writes; explicit generation may prepare/download pinned plugins. |
| go_version / go_missing | Select Go 1.27.2 or newer on PATH; dev never downloads a toolchain. |
| Missing module/checksum | Prepare dependencies explicitly. First local use tidies the root CLI module and retains go.work. For isolated service tidy/build, publish/select actual contracts and set GOWORK=off. Never disguise an unpublished module with a production replace. |
| Orders returns 503 | Check Identity target, TLS and readiness. RPC deadlines remain bounded; do not hide mutating failures with automatic retries. |
| Worker exits immediately | Any unexpected child exit, including status zero, stops siblings and returns non-zero. |

No dotenv loading, implicit discovery, required database or central runtime is added. Unix uses process groups. Windows uses Job Objects, attempts console break and uses bounded termination if a console signal is unavailable. Forced termination does not guarantee application callbacks finished cleanup.

title: Microservices
description: Develop independent Go services with explicit typed clients, local diagnostics and supervised processes.
text:
Project home(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex) · Documentation index(/docs/main/)

Follow First mapped microservice call(/docs/main/microservices-quickstart/) to install the public CLI, generate independent services, make caller-owned business edits and run with one command after explicit dependency preparation. Monolith remains the simplest default.

Services retain separate go.mod/main.go/config/modules and HTTP/gRPC/mixed/worker listener profiles. Business services use plain Go interfaces; client/transport adapters own protocol mapping. Persistence is optional and belongs to each service.

The strict caller-editable gonex.yaml owns local paths, loopback addresses and declared client edges. go.mod owns versions; .gonex.json owns generator metadata. No secrets, discovery or runtime global injection live in this catalog.

Use doctor then dev with explicit --dev-insecure for local plaintext, or configure real TLS/mTLS. dev builds cached dependencies and supervises direct binaries with prefixed output; it never silently tidies modules or downloads tools. --service starts only the selected process. Logs/readiness confirm availability; configured addresses alone do not.

Client skeletons intentionally fail compilation until mapping/wiring is complete. The example profile supports only the verified starter contract; raw retains manual typed-client bootstrap. Publish actual contracts and pin versions before GOWORK=off deployment. go.work is local convenience, not a deployment dependency.

See compatibility(/docs/main/microservices-compatibility/), troubleshooting(/docs/main/microservices-troubleshooting/), acceptance(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/microservices-dx/acceptance.md) and the advanced Identity/Orders example(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/tree/main/examples/microservices). Its labeled source replacements are distinct from the new independently resolved public tutorial.

title: Modules and lifecycle
description: Register explicit Go modules, share business services, and manage resources through startup and graceful shutdown.
text:
Register a module

A module implements Register(app.Registrar) error. Registration declares routes, managed resources and named readiness checks; it should not open listeners or databases. Register related modules together when their declarations must succeed atomically. Registration seals before startup, and retained registrars cannot mutate a running app.

 Keep business logic independent

Keep business services in modules/NAME/service.go. They accept context and domain values and depend on small interfaces owned by their consumer. HTTP schemas/handlers, Protobuf mappers and GORM adapters translate at the boundary. Avoid a shared repository that exposes another service's database.

 Share services across adapters

Generated modules expose an injectable service and NewModuleService; generated registries create one service for all its adapters. Change business logic in handwritten files. Tool-owned registries are hash-checked and must be reconciled explicitly if manually edited.

 Manage resources

Use Registrar.Manage for resources implementing Start(context.Context) error and Close(context.Context) error. Dependencies register before their consumers: database, client pool, then server. Startup failure closes resources already started; shutdown drains HTTP and closes resources in reverse order. Resources can expose an Errors() <-chan error channel for asynchronous failure; App.Run then stops the application and returns an error. Resources must honor their lifecycle contexts.

 Own background work

Start is explicit, Run waits for cancellation/failure, and Shutdown is idempotent. A stopped application cannot restart. Do not start unmanaged goroutines from registration: own their cancellation and join them from a resource's Close method. See operations(/docs/main/operations/) for health checks and shutdown behavior.

title: Metrics and tracing
description: Correlate Gonex request logs and unary RPC traces, collect bounded latency histograms and opt in to Prometheus metrics.
text:
Correlate requests

Default request logging now includes service, environment, request_id and trace_id. The server returns X-Request-ID and a validated W3C traceparent. Pass the request context into services to retain correlation. HTTP-to-gRPC unary instrumentation preserves the trace ID; streaming instrumentation and an OTLP span exporter are not declared supported.

 Opt in to metrics

Install observability.HTTP(metrics) through application middleware and manage the Metrics resource in your module. Metrics collect requests, errors, in-flight work and cumulative latency buckets. Each collector retains at most 128 operation labels, including overflow; labels are limited to 160 bytes and must not contain control characters. Use fixed route/RPC patterns, never user IDs or raw URLs.

Finite histogram boundaries are 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, 2500 and 5000 milliseconds, plus +Inf. Snapshots are concurrency safe. The default application requires no metrics backend.

 Export to Prometheus

The optional github.com/amkargar/gonex/observability/prometheus package supplies Handler(metrics). Mount this standard net/http handler deliberately on a protected operational route/listener. It emits Prometheus text 0.0.4 and starts no network client or exporter worker. A disconnected monitoring backend cannot block API requests through a push exporter because none is started.

The diagnostic source example(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/tree/main/examples/observability) demonstrates a dependency failure, 503 readiness, correlated logs and counters/histograms, followed by recovery. The executable is a maintainer demonstration; install Gonex in your own application using the CLI guide(/docs/main/quick-start/).

 Privacy and cost

Default logs/labels exclude bodies, tokens, headers, query strings and raw unmatched paths. Nonstandard method tokens use OTHER. Application-defined fields remain your responsibility. Custom writers/readiness callbacks must honor their contracts; arbitrary callbacks cannot be forcibly interrupted safely.

Core and telemetry overhead are measured separately, including paced loopback workloads and CPU/heap profiles. Review the readiness evidence(/docs/main/production-readiness/) before treating short CI results as deployment SLOs.

title: Operations and readiness
description: Configure readiness, graceful shutdown, request metrics, resource ownership and trace propagation.
text:
Structured logs

The application emits lifecycle and request logs by default. See Server output and logging(/docs/main/logging/) for configuration, startup URLs and request IDs. Trace propagation and metrics below are independently opt-in.

 Health and readiness

/healthz reports that HTTP is serving. /readyz returns 200 only while the application is running and its managed readiness resources and named checks succeed; otherwise it returns a redacted 503. Registrar.Check(name, func(context.Context) error) registers an application-specific check. Checks share a one-second budget and must honor context. The GORM resource pings its pool; the gRPC server checks its transport lifecycle. Check downstream RPC availability explicitly with Clients.Ready, rather than assuming a constructed client is connected.

 Propagate trace context

observability.HTTP(metrics) is optional Gin middleware installed through config.Config.Middleware. It accepts valid version-00 traceparent headers, preserves the trace ID and creates a new span ID. Invalid/duplicate headers start a fresh trace. observability.Traceparent(ctx) reads the current value. Optional observability/grpc.Client and Server unary interceptors propagate it across services; credentials and arbitrary incoming metadata are not forwarded. Streaming trace propagation and an OTLP exporter are not implemented.

 Collect metrics

observability.NewMetrics() is a managed resource. Counters track completed requests, errors, in-flight work and cumulative elapsed nanoseconds by fixed route/RPC name. Unknown HTTP URLs share an unmatched label; raw URLs, user IDs and secrets are excluded. SnapshotContext copies measurements for a caller-owned exporter. Call SetReadiness(application.Ready) to include dependency readiness; without that callback, readiness represents the metrics resource's lifecycle only. Snapshots now include bounded cumulative duration histograms; opt-in Prometheus exporting and trace correlation are described in Metrics and tracing(/docs/main/observability/). No external backend is required.

 Expose example metrics

The basic example enables tracing/counters and exposes its JSON metrics route only with GONEX_EXPOSE_METRICS=1. Protect that route at your deployment boundary if enabled. There is no exporter endpoint by default in framework applications.

 Drain and stop services

Shutdown first stops accepting HTTP traffic and drains active requests within the shutdown budget, then closes managed resources in reverse order. gRPC uses graceful stop with a forced stop when its context expires. Signal handling belongs to the executable. HTTP deadline middleware cancels request contexts; handlers and dependency calls must honor them. A handler that ignores context cannot be forcibly interrupted safely.

 Verify your application

Run go tool gonex check from your generated project and test your public endpoints. Probe /healthz and /readyz separately, verify dependency-failure behavior, and allow shutdown time in your process manager. Framework regression tests belong in Contribute: testing(/docs/main/contribute/testing/).

title: Production readiness
description: Review Gonex hardening, the standalone PostgreSQL API sample, verification evidence and the remaining production release gates.
text:
Implementation and evidence

Gonex now includes repeatable quality/security/fuzz gates, real PostgreSQL fault tests, cross-process migration checks, bounded telemetry, load/profile tooling, lifecycle regressions and a standalone Orders API rehearsal. The minimum patched toolchain is Go 1.27.2.

This is a development snapshot, not a declaration that all production-release gates have closed. Read the current final report(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/production-readiness/final-report.md) and its linked CI evidence for the actual decision. A configured workflow alone is not a successful hosted run.

 Independent service example

The Orders API source(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/tree/main/examples/production) has its own go.mod pinned to a public framework commit, with no local replace/workspace dependency. It demonstrates authenticated create/list/get/update/delete operations, role-based write authorization, validation, offset pagination/status filtering, explicit SQL migrations and OpenAPI.

Its Docker Compose rehearsal starts PostgreSQL and migration/API containers, tests API workflows, interrupts the database, verifies unready behavior and recovery, and checks retained data. Secrets are caller-provided; no default production tokens are generated. Plain database transport is restricted to the disposable private rehearsal network, not a production TLS policy.

 Release gates that still need evidence

- Enforced branch checks and a demonstrated blocked failing PR require repository-owner configuration.
- Private disclosure activation, independent security review and onboarding by an unfamiliar developer require external confirmation.
- A stable/tagged install, signed tag artifacts and a prior-release upgrade/rollback need a reviewed candidate and release decision.
- Short hosted load/soak probes do not certify deployment hardware, production TLS/PostgreSQL latency, long-term maintenance or incident history.

 Deploy deliberately

Use the deployment guide(/docs/main/deployment/), security guide(/docs/main/security/) and logging configuration(/docs/main/logging/). The upstream promotion checklist(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/production-checklist.md), support policy(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/support-policy.md) and troubleshooting guide(https://github.com/amkargar/gonex/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md) define operational scope and responsibilities. Do not infer a 10/10 maturity claim from initial technical gates.

title: Organize your API project
description: Develop inside a CLI-generated Gonex application with clear service, schema, handler and route responsibilities and protected registries.
text:
The generated layout

Start with gonex new shop --module example.com/acme/shop, then go mod tidy and go tool gonex create module users inside shop:

text
shop/
├── go.mod
├── go.sum
├── main.go
├── .gonex.json
├── config/
│   └── config.go
└── modules/
    ├── registry_gen.go
    └── users/
        ├── module.go
        ├── service.go
        ├── service_test.go
        ├── http_registry_gen.go
        └── http/
            ├── schemas.go
            ├── handlers.go
            ├── routes.go
            └── openapi.go


go.mod tracks Gonex as the runtime library and CLI development tool. The server has no application HTML/CSS scaffold. HTTP API versioning, database files and gRPC adapters appear only when requested.

 Files you edit

- main.go: application construction, explicit modules and signal handling.
- config/config.go: environment/configuration mapping, logging and exposure settings.
- module.go: service construction and adapter wiring.
- service.go: plain Go business behavior and local interfaces.
- schemas.go: HTTP DTOs and validation tags.
- handlers.go: request-to-service calls and response mapping.
- routes.go and openapi.go: typed routes and contract descriptions.
- Tests: verify your application's domain and API behavior.

These are application files owned by you. The CLI does not continuously regenerate your service logic. A starter module exposes a message endpoint; implementing resource actions is deliberate development, as shown in Build a REST API(/docs/main/building-api/).

 Tool-owned files

Keep .gonex.json, modules/registry_gen.go, and generated adapter registries under tool ownership. Generators hash-check these files and reject conflicting manual edits. Use commands to add modules, enable transports and create versions. When changing a handwritten adapter's interface, update its module wiring deliberately rather than breaking a generated registry's assumptions.

 Keep developing

sh
go tool gonex create module products
go tool gonex check
go tool gonex run


A separate frontend consumes the API over HTTP. Optional database adapters and models stay at the module boundary; migration execution remains explicit.

title: Your first API project
description: Create a Gonex project with the CLI, add an HTTP module, run the server and inspect JSON responses, logs and OpenAPI.
text:
Install the CLI

sh
go install github.com/amkargar/gonex/cmd/gonex@3ca54b46cb42


Use Go 1.27.2 and put Go's binary directory on PATH. See installation(/docs/main/installation/) for details. This is a pinned development snapshot, not a stable release.

 Create your application

sh
gonex new shop --module example.com/acme/shop
cd shop
go mod tidy


You now have your own Go application: main.go, config/, modules/, a pinned framework dependency and a project-local CLI tool. No framework clone or Git commands are part of this setup.

 Add an HTTP module

sh
go tool gonex create module users


HTTP is the default transport. This creates a small editable JSON endpoint at /users plus service, handler, schemas and route files. There is no database, gRPC or HTTP API version requirement.

 Run and inspect the server

sh
go tool gonex check
go tool gonex run


The terminal displays the actual bound server URL, environment, Gonex version, OpenAPI URL and Ctrl+C instructions after a successful start. Each request emits a completion log with request ID, route, status and elapsed milliseconds. Configure logs(/docs/main/logging/) for readable development output or production JSON.

From another terminal:

sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/users
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/openapi.json


The module returns:

json
"message":"users"


The response header X-Request-ID matches the request's log correlation ID. Stop with Ctrl+C to drain requests and close resources.

 See the development welcome page

Enable debug mode in the process running your application:

sh
DEBUG=true go tool gonex run


On PowerShell:

powershell
$env:DEBUG = "true"
go tool gonex run


Visit http://127.0.0.1:8080/ for Welcome to Gonex, the duck mascot, website
and documentation links. A matching application root route takes priority.
Browser errors show diagnostics; JSON clients keep their API response format.
Use DEBUG=false for public deployments. Debug mode details(/docs/main/debug/).

 Know where to write code

| File | Your responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| modules/users/service.go | Business behavior, plain Go inputs and results |
| modules/users/http/schemas.go | Request/response DTOs and validation |
| modules/users/http/handlers.go | Request-to-service mapping |
| modules/users/http/routes.go | Endpoint methods, paths and statuses |
| modules/users/http/openapi.go | API descriptions |
| modules/users/module.go | Service construction and adapter wiring |

Edit these handwritten files inside your app. Keep .gonex.json and generated registries tool-owned. Generators refuse to overwrite existing module code.

 Continue with a real resource API

The starter response demonstrates the structure; it is not generated CRUD. Continue with Build a REST API(/docs/main/building-api/) for create/list/get users, JSON validation, conflict/not-found errors and OpenAPI. That guide starts from a separate generated project so its custom users module does not conflict with this starter.

Project structure(/docs/main/project-structure/) explains ownership; CLI reference(/docs/main/cli/) covers optional database, versioned HTTP and gRPC commands.

 Need independent services?

The monolith remains the simplest default. Follow First microservice call(/docs/main/microservices-quickstart/) when you need independent services; no framework clone is required.

title: Release status
description: Understand the current Gonex development snapshot, dependency pinning and support considerations for application developers.
text:
Development snapshot

The reviewed framework source has no published release. These guides target a particular main commit and show how to pin it as a Go dependency. Do not assume a version mentioned by a generator default is available from a module proxy.

 Choose a dependency deliberately

Use the installation guide(/docs/main/installation/) to pin the reviewed commit. When release tags become available, select an actual published version and review its changelog, compatibility notes and verification record before upgrading.

 Verify your application environment

The upstream release policy describes configured verification targets and outstanding checks; configured targets alone do not prove runtime support. Check your own operating system, database, TLS/proxy configuration and resource lifecycles. See deployment(/docs/main/deployment/) and security(/docs/main/security/).

 Looking for the maintainer checklist?

Framework CI gates, contracts-module releases, generated baselines and release preparation belong in Contribute to Gonex → Maintaining releases(/docs/main/contribute/releases/).

 Production-readiness evidence

Review the hardening status and open release gates(/docs/main/production-readiness/). Technical implementation, a green CI run and an independently reviewed production release are separate milestones.

title: Security configuration
description: Review Gonex request limits, authentication boundaries, CORS policy and secure transport configuration.
text:
Authentication and authorization

Authentication is application-owned. security.Authenticate(verifier) delegates credential extraction and verification, requires a nonempty subject and returns a generic 401 on failure. security.Current(ctx) reads the principal. security.Authorize(predicate) returns 403 for a rejected authenticated principal. Install authentication before authorization. Declare matching endpoint error statuses and OpenAPI security schemes; metadata alone does not enforce authentication. No JWT/session scheme is assumed.

 CORS policy

No CORS middleware is enabled automatically. security.CORS accepts explicit HTTP(S) origins, methods and header allowlists, validates configuration and denies unknown origins/preflights. Wildcards are rejected. Credentials are opt-in; preflight caching is limited to 24 hours. CORS does not replace authentication or CSRF defenses for cookie-based applications.

 Request limits and deadlines

Typed bodies default to 1 MiB and reject unknown fields, duplicate keys, trailing JSON, incorrect field case and null nonnullable values. Parameter duplicates and nonfinite floats are rejected. Use pointer DTO fields for optional/presence-sensitive values and pointer nested input objects. Set MaxBodyBytes for an endpoint and http.Deadline for cooperative request deadlines. Server defaults are read 10s, write 30s, idle 60s and shutdown 10s. Configure ingress and application budgets together.

 Transport security

The HTTP listener is plain HTTP intended for a configured TLS ingress or private local deployment. gRPC requires TLS 1.2 or newer; loading helpers support CA verification and mTLS. Plaintext requires explicit DevelopmentInsecure; clients reject skipped certificate verification. No automatic RPC retries are enabled. Managed clients apply a five-second default unary/stream deadline, bounded by an earlier caller deadline.

 Error and secret redaction

With debug disabled, internal errors, panic payloads, readiness failures and database startup credentials are redacted at framework boundaries. JSON clients retain generic internal errors even in debug mode. Browser HTML diagnostics with DEBUG=true can display original errors and stacks; use DEBUG=false on public deployments and see debug mode(/docs/main/debug/). Recovery does not dump request headers or panic values. Application logs, SQL logging, explicit public error messages and caller-supplied interceptors remain the application's responsibility. Trace identifiers are correlation data, never authentication credentials.

 Documentation and metrics exposure

OpenAPI is enabled by default: set DisableOpenAPI when it should not be public. /docs is opt-in and loads no external assets. Trusted proxies are disabled unless configured outside the framework's router. Metrics exposure is opt-in in the example. Load secrets from deployment configuration; do not commit credentials.

title: Compatibility and upgrades
description: Pin Gonex versions and review HTTP, Protobuf and generated-code compatibility before upgrading.
text:
Module version policy

goNex uses semantic module versions. Until v1, minor versions may change APIs and templates; patch versions should preserve behavior except documented bug/security fixes. Review the changelog, pin the framework version and upgrade in a branch. No automatic migration of handwritten code is provided.

 Upgrade checklist

1. Update the framework requirement and run go mod tidy independently in each service.
2. Review DTO validation, lifecycle behavior and generated registries before regenerating. .gonex.json format 1 records hashes; generators refuse changed owned files and incompatible layouts. Resolve conflicts explicitly rather than deleting metadata.
3. Run tests, vet, build, migration checks and contract generation/checks. Database migrations are ordered immutable files: append a migration instead of editing applied SQL. Take deployment-specific backups before applying schema changes.
4. Export every supported HTTP version and compare its release baseline. Deploy consumers/providers in a compatible order before retiring old contracts.

 HTTP compatibility

HTTP compatibility includes methods/paths, operation IDs, parameter locations/types/requiredness, body schemas, response status/schema and security requirements. gonex openapi validate --file current.json --against baseline.json performs a conservative comparison: additions are allowed but changes to existing contracts are rejected, including some harmless descriptive edits. Review such changes explicitly; do not silently replace the baseline. Keep separate baselines for each HTTP major. See versioning(/docs/main/versioning/).

 Protobuf compatibility

Protobuf packages encode the API major (identity.v1). Keep field numbers/types, service/method identities and request/response types compatible. Run both gonex grpc check and Buf breaking against the released descriptor baseline. Removing/repurposing fields or methods requires a new version and a consumer migration. The internal checker is deliberately conservative; Buf is an additional release gate.

 Strict DTO changes

This implementation tightens early-phase behavior: duplicate JSON keys and unsupported validation tags now fail; nested request objects require pointers; custom JSON encodings require explicit transport DTOs. A value body wrapper is already required and should not carry validate:"required"; use a pointer if the body's explicit presence is validated. Deadline failures have a documented 504 response. These changes prevent runtime/schema disagreement; update DTOs rather than weakening exported contracts.

 Template compatibility

Templates do not infer business mappings. Older module layouts require the injectable service factory before automatic gRPC enable. Existing handwritten adapters are retained when versions are added; --policy replace is an explicit legacy-route registration change.

title: HTTP API versions
description: Keep version-specific HTTP adapters and contracts separate while sharing business behavior in Gonex.
text:
Add an HTTP version

sh
gonex module version users --http v1 --policy preserve --dry-run
gonex module version users --http v1
gonex module version users --http v2


 Preserve or replace legacy routes

The default preserve policy retains existing handlers and URLs. Adapter sources are copied into independent http/v1 and http/v2 packages; generated registration calls them with one shared service instance. Handwritten handlers, service/repository/model files and prior version packages are untouched. Reruns fail without overwriting. Resolve an edited generated registry before retrying.

--policy replace explicitly stops registering legacy routes, while retaining their source files. That choice persists when later versions are added. No command deletes v1. Deprecation and retirement are application decisions; announce retirement and remove old registrations only as an explicit breaking change.

 Choose a prefix

Default prefixes are /api/v1, /api/v2. Use --prefix /custom/v1 when generating, or http.WithVersion(registrar,"v1",prefix) when registering manually. Versions are positive major identifiers (v1, v2, ...), never v0 or arbitrary path fragments. Version registration changes the typed contract and runtime path together, adds an operation-ID suffix and refuses collisions.

 Export independent contracts

/openapi.json describes legacy routes. /openapi/v1.json and /openapi/v2.json describe their respective effective paths and independent schemas; each document validates against OpenAPI 3.1. App.OpenAPIVersion("v1") exports a registered document without listening and rejects unknown versions. All public documents are disabled together with DisableOpenAPI. CLI export defaults to the legacy document; select a version with gonex openapi generate --http-version v1 --out v1.json.

 Start with a versioned module

Create an initially versioned module with gonex create module catalog --http-version v1. This profile starts directly with http/v1 and does not register legacy routes. Compare each released document using gonex openapi validate --file current.json --against baseline.json; see compatibility policy(/docs/main/upgrades/).

 Handle custom adapter layouts

Version generation expects the Phase 4 adapter Register signature and generated HTTP registry hook. Custom adapter layouts/signatures may require a manual registration change; conflicts must be resolved before generation. Copying a version does not infer a new business API: edit its schemas and handlers to define the intended compatibility boundary.
